crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Expense Fraud
children.blurb: Expense fraud covers duplicate claims, inflated amounts, personal costs submitted as business expenses, fictitious receipts, and collusion between employees and approvers or vendors.

children.name: Money Laundering Networks
children.blurb: Money laundering networks are groups of individuals, shell companies, accounts, and transactions arranged to move illicit funds while obscuring origin and ownership.

children.name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
children.blurb: Phantom vendors are supplier records that exist only on paper or in a system, created to route payments to a fraudster rather than a real provider of goods or services.

children.name: Communication Forensics
children.blurb: Communication forensics applies analytical methods to emails, chat logs, call recordings, and other message data to uncover fraud, reconstruct events, and support investigations.

children.name: Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets
children.blurb: Tracing and recovering digital assets covers the identification, location, and legal recovery of funds or tokenized property that have been moved through cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, decentralized finance protocols, and other digital channels.

sections.body: Fraud detection and forensics applies machine learning to find suspicious patterns in financial records, communications, and asset movements. In practice, AI systems now flag expense claims that deviate from an employee's own history or from peer norms, and they scan invoices for signs of shell companies or duplicate billing. They also parse email and chat logs for language that suggests collusion or concealment, and they follow cryptocurrency transfers across public ledgers. This is not a future vision, it is routine work inside banks, insurers, audit firms, and corporate finance teams. The tools are narrow, they look for specific signatures rather than understanding fraud in a human sense.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most mature area is expense fraud, where supervised models trained on labeled past cases can catch many common abuses, but they still miss novel schemes and generate false alarms that require human review. Money laundering detection has improved at linking entities through shared addresses, phone numbers, and transaction timing, yet it struggles with layered corporate structures and jurisdictions that do not share data. Phantom vendor detection works well when procurement records are clean and complete, but real-world vendor files are often messy, duplicated, or missing key fields. Communication forensics can surface unusual phrasing or hidden relationships, but it cannot reliably infer intent, and its output is only one input to an investigation. Across the 732 AI tools this site tracks, the honest limit is that none of them replace a forensic accountant or a lawyer, they reduce the haystack but do not remove it.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Expense Fraud to see the most common and best documented use of AI in this section, then move to Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud for the adjacent problem of fake suppliers and bid rigging. Money Laundering Networks covers the harder, more relational side of the field, where graph based methods try to expose hidden groups rather than single bad actors. Communication Forensics shifts from money to words, showing how AI reads emails, chats, and call transcripts for signs of coordination or cover up. Tracing and Recovering Digital Assets closes the loop by following stolen or hidden funds across blockchains and exchanges, which is often the last step after the other pages have identified a suspect or a scheme. Together the five pages move from individual wrongdoing to networks, then from financial records to language, and finally to asset movement.
